source_text: Οὐκοῦν ἄπλετος ἡ τοῦ ὕδατος φύσις τῇ γῇ περιεκέχυτο, οὐχὶ συμμέτρως ἔχουσα πρὸς αὐτὴν, ἀλλ' εἰς τὸ πολλαπλάσιον ὑπερβάλλουσα, οὕτως ἐξ ἀρχῆς τοῦ μεγάλου τεχνίτου προβλεψαμένου τὸ μέλλον, καὶ διὰ τὴν ἐφεξῆς χρείαν τὰ πρῶτα διαθεμένου. Τίς οὖν χρεία τοῦ ἀμύθητον ὅσον ὑπερβάλλειν τὸ ὕδωρ; Ἐπειδὴ ἀναγκαία τῷ παντὶ τοῦ πυρὸς ἡ οὐσία, οὐ μόνον πρὸς τὴν τῶν περιγείων οἰκονομίαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τὴν συμπλήρωσιν τοῦ παντός. Κολοβὸν γὰρ ἂν ἦν τὸ ὅλον ἑνὶ τῷ μεγίστῳ καὶ καιριωτάτῳ πάντων ἐλλεῖπον. Ἀντικείμενα δὲ ταῦτα ἀλλήλοις, καὶ φθαρτικὸν ἕτερον τοῦ ἑτέρου· πῦρ μὲν τοῦ ὕδατος, ὅταν ἐπικρατῇ δυνάμει· ὕδωρ δὲ πυρὸς, ὅταν ὑπερβάλλῃ τῷ πλήθει. Ἔδει δὲ μήτε στάσιν εἶναι πρὸς ἄλληλα, μήτε ἐν τῇ παντελεῖ τοῦ ἑτέρου ἐκλείψει ἀφορμὴν παρασχεθῆναι τῷ παντὶ πρὸς διάλυσιν. Τοσαύτην τοῦ ὑγροῦ τὴν φύσιν οἰκονομῶν τὸ πᾶν προαπέθετο, ὥστε μέχρι τῶν τεταγμένων ὅρων τῆς τοῦ κόσμου συστάσεως κατὰ μικρὸν τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ πυρὸς ἐξαναλισκόμενον ἀντισχεῖν. Ὁ τοίνυν ἅπαντα σταθμῷ καὶ μέτρῳ διαταξάμενος (ἀριθμηταὶ γὰρ αὐτῷ, κατὰ τὸν Ἰὼβ, καὶ σταγόνες εἰσὶν ὑετοῦ) ᾔδει πόσον τῷ κόσμῳ χρόνον ἀφώρισεν εἰς διαμονὴν, καὶ πόσην χρὴ τῷ πυρὶ προαποθέσθαι δαπάνην. Οὗτος ὁ λόγος τῆς τοῦ ὕδατος περιουσίας κατὰ τὴν κτίσιν. Ἀλλὰ μὴν τό γε τοῦ πυρὸς ἀναγκαῖον τῷ κόσμῳ, οὐδεὶς οὕτως ἔξω τοῦ βίου παντάπασιν, ὥστε τῆς ἐκ τοῦ λόγου διδασκαλίας προσδεῖσθαι· οὐ μόνον ὅτι αἱ συνεκτικαὶ τῆς ζωῆς ἡμῶν τέχναι τῆς ἐμπύρου ἐργασίας ἐπιδέονται πᾶσαι, ὑφαντικὴ, λέγω, καὶ σκυτοτομικὴ, καὶ οἰκοδομικὴ, καὶ γεωργία, ἀλλ' ὅτι οὔτε δένδρων βλάστησις, οὐ καρπῶν πέψις, οὐ ζῴων ἐγγείων ἢ τῶν ἐνύδρων γένεσις, οὐχ αἱ τούτων τροφαὶ ἢ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἂν συνέστησαν, ἢ πρὸς χρόνον διήρκεσαν, τοῦ θερμοῦ μὴ παρόντος. Οὐκοῦν ἀναγκαία μὲν τοῦ θερμοῦ ἡ κτίσις διὰ τὴν τῶν γιγνομένων σύστασίν τε καὶ διαμονήν· ἀναγκαία δὲ τοῦ ὑγροῦ ἡ δαψίλεια διὰ τὸ ἄπαυστον εἶναι καὶ ἀπαραίτητον τοῦ πυρὸς τὴν δαπάνην. 3.6 Περίβλεψαι πᾶσαν τὴν κτίσιν, καὶ ὄψει τοῦ θερμοῦ τὴν δύναμιν τοῖς ἐν γενέσει καὶ φθορᾷ πᾶσιν ἐνδυναστεύουσαν. Διὰ τοῦτο πολὺ τὸ ὕδωρ ὑπὲρ γῆς κεχυμένον, καὶ ὑπερέκεινα τῶν ὁρωμένων ἀπενεχθὲν, καὶ προσέτι παντὶ τῷ βάθει τῆς γῆς ἐνεσπαρμένον. Ὅθεν πηγῶν ἀφθονίαι, καὶ φρεάτων σύρροιαι, καὶ ποταμῶν ῥεύματα, χειμάρρων τε καὶ ἀεννάων, ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἐν πολλοῖς καὶ ποικίλοις ταμείοις διατηρεῖσθαι τὴν ὑγρασίαν. Ἐκ μέν γε τῆς ἕω, ἀπὸ μὲν χειμερινῶν τροπῶν ὁ Ἰνδὸς ῥεῖ ποταμὸς ῥεῦμα πάντων ποταμίων ὑδάτων πλεῖστον, ὡς οἱ τὰς περιόδους τῆς γῆς ἀναγράφοντες ἱστορήκασιν· ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν μέσων τῆς ἀνατολῆς ὅ τε Βάκτρος, καὶ ὁ Χοάσπης, καὶ ὁ Ἀράξης, ἀφ' οὗ καὶ ὁ Τάναϊς ἀποσχιζόμενος εἰς τὴν Μαιῶτιν ἔξεισι λίμνην. Καὶ πρὸς τούτοις ὁ Φάσις τῶν Καυκασίων ὀρῶν ἀπορρέων, καὶ μυρίοι ἕτεροι ἀπὸ τῶν ἀρκτῴων τόπων ἐπὶ τὸν Εὔξεινον Πόντον φέρονται. Ἀπὸ δὲ δυσμῶν τῶν θερινῶν ὑπὸ τὸ Πυρηναῖον ὄρος Ταρτησός τε καὶ Ἴστρος· ὧν ὁ μὲν ἐπὶ τὴν ἔξω Στηλῶν ἀφίεται θάλασσαν· ὁ δὲ Ἴστρος διὰ τῆς Εὐρώπης ῥέων, ἐπὶ τὸν Πόντον ἐκδίδωσι.
thought_title: Why the waters were created in such abundance
orientation: Basil is explaining why the earth was initially covered with far more water than it needed, arguing that the excess was stored up to fuel the sun's fire over the whole duration of the world.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore the boundless nature of the water had been poured around the earth, not having a proportionate amount in relation to it, but exceeding it to a multiple degree, since from the beginning the great craftsman foresaw the future, and because of the subsequent need arranged the first things. What then is the need for the water to exceed by an unspeakable amount? Because the substance of fire is necessary for the whole, not only for the management of the things around the earth, but also for the completion of the whole. For the whole would have been maimed, lacking one of the greatest and most vital of all things. But these are opposed to each other, and each is destructive of the other: fire of water, whenever it prevails in power; and water of fire, whenever it exceeds in quantity. But it was necessary neither that there be conflict between them, nor that by the complete failure of one an occasion be given to the whole for dissolution. The one who manages the whole stored up in advance such a nature of the moist, so that until the appointed limits of the constitution of the world, being consumed little by little by the power of the fire, it might hold out. The one therefore who arranged all things by weight and measure (for the drops of rain are numbered to him, according to Job) knew how much time he had marked off for the world for its continuance, and how much expenditure it was necessary to store up in advance for the fire. This is the reason for the abundance of water at the creation. But indeed that the substance of fire is necessary for the world, no one is so entirely outside of life as to need instruction from this discourse; not only because all the arts that hold our life together need the fiery working—weaving, I mean, and leather-working, and house-building, and farming—but because neither the sprouting of trees, nor the ripening of fruits, nor the generation of land animals or of water animals, nor their nourishment would either have been constituted from the beginning, or would have lasted for a time, if the hot were not present. Therefore the creation of the hot is necessary for the constitution and continuance of the things that come to be; and the abundance of the moist is necessary because the expenditure of the fire is unceasing and unavoidable. Look around at the whole creation, and you will see the power of the hot ruling over all things that are in generation and corruption. For this reason much water has been poured over the earth, and carried away beyond the things that are seen, and in addition sown throughout the whole depth of the earth. Whence come abundances of springs, and flows of wells, and currents of rivers, both winter-flowing and ever-flowing, so that the moisture might be preserved in many and varied storehouses. From the east, from the winter solstice flows the Indus river, the greatest flow of all river waters, as those who record the circuits of the earth have related; and from the middle parts of the east the Bactrus, and the Choaspes, and the Araxes, from which also the Tanais, splitting off, goes out into the Sea of Azov. And in addition to these the Phasis, flowing down from the Caucasian mountains, and countless others from the northern regions are carried to the Black Sea. And from the west of the summer solstice, under the Pyrenean mountain, the Tartessus and the Ister; of which the one is sent forth to the sea outside the Pillars; and the Ister, flowing through Europe, empties into the Black Sea.

choices.english: the boundless nature of the water
choices.why: Keeps the adjective 'boundless' with 'nature' to preserve the emphasis on the water's excessive quantity, which is Basil's point.
Renders τεχνίτης literally as 'craftsman' to preserve Basil's image of God as a deliberate artisan, matching the brief's emphasis on deliberate making.
Keeps the rhetorical force of 'unspeakable' to convey the vast excess Basil stresses.

choices.term: Κολοβὸν γὰρ ἂν ἦν τὸ ὅλον
choices.english: For the whole would have been maimed
choices.why: Renders κολοβός as 'maimed' to preserve the vivid image of incompleteness or mutilation.
rejected: the whole would have been incomplete
the whole would have been defective

choices.why: Keeps the verb's sense of exercising power or dominion, fitting Basil's point about heat's pervasive force.
Renders ταμεῖον as 'storehouses' to preserve the image of the earth's depths as reservoirs for moisture.

pass_b_english: So the boundless nature of the water had been poured around the earth, not in proportion to it, but exceeding it many times over. From the beginning the great craftsman foresaw what was to come and arranged the first things for the need that would follow. What need was there, then, for the water to exceed by an unspeakable amount? Because the substance of fire is necessary to the whole—not only for the ordering of things around the earth, but also for the completion of the universe. For the whole would have been maimed if it lacked the one greatest and most vital element of all. These two are opposed to each other, and each is destructive of the other: fire destroys water when it prevails by force, and water destroys fire when it exceeds in quantity. But there had to be neither a standoff between them nor any occasion given to the universe for dissolution through the complete failure of one of them. The One who orders all things arranged in advance such a quantity of the moist nature that, as it is gradually consumed by the power of fire, it would hold out until the appointed limits of the world's duration. For the One who arranged all things by weight and measure—since, according to Job, even the drops of rain are numbered by him (Job 38:37 (LXX))—knew how much time he had marked off for the world to endure, and how much expenditure he needed to set aside in advance for the fire. This is the reason for the abundance of water at creation.

But surely no one is so entirely outside of life as to need instruction from this discourse that fire is necessary to the world. Not only because all the crafts that sustain our lives require the work of fire—I mean weaving, leather-working, building, and farming—but because neither the sprouting of trees, nor the ripening of fruits, nor the generation of land animals or water creatures, nor their nourishment, would ever have come into being in the beginning or endured over time if heat were absent. So the creation of heat is necessary for the formation and continuance of things that come into being, and the abundance of moisture is necessary because the consumption of fire is unceasing and unavoidable.

Look around at the whole creation, and you will see the power of heat ruling over everything that comes into being and decays. For this reason much water was poured over the earth, carried beyond the visible regions, and in addition sown throughout the entire depth of the earth. From there come abundant springs, the gathering of wells, the streams of rivers—both winter torrents and ever-flowing ones—so that the moisture is preserved in many and varied storehouses. From the east, from the winter solstice, flows the Indus River, the greatest stream of all river waters, as those who have written accounts of the earth's regions have recorded. From the middle of the east flow the Bactrus, the Choaspes, and the Araxes, from which the Tanais branches off and empties into the Sea of Azov. And besides these, the Phasis flows down from the Caucasus Mountains, and countless other rivers from the northern regions rush toward the Black Sea. From the west, from the summer solstice, beneath the Pyrenees, flow the Tartessus and the Ister. One of these pours into the sea beyond the Pillars of Hercules, while the Ister flows through Europe and empties into the Black Sea.

fixed: Changed 'at the start' to 'in the beginning' to avoid the banned rendering of ἐν ἀρχῇ; the source phrase ἐξ ἀρχῆς here refers to the original constitution of things, and the glossary requires 'in the beginning'.

last_rejected.why: Basil quotes Job on numbered drops of rain; LXX Job 38:37 does not match. LXX Job 36:27 or 38:28 better fit.
last_rejected.ruling: Source only says 'κατὰ τὸν Ἰὼβ'; exact verse reference is translator's annotation, not a mistranslation of the text.

last_rejected.why: δυνάμει means 'in power/powerfully,' not 'by force.' Fire destroys water when it prevails in power.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Prevails by force' is within normal range of ἐπικρατῇ δυνάμει; 'in power' is a preference, not an error.

last_rejected.quote: the one greatest and most vital element of all
last_rejected.source_quote: ἑνὶ τῷ μεγίστῳ καὶ καιριωτάτῳ πάντων
last_rejected.why: ἐλλεῖπον takes dative: 'lacking the one greatest...' but 'element' is added; καιριωτάτῳ means 'most critical/essential,' not 'most vital.'

last_rejected.ruling: 'Element' is reasonable contextual sense; 'vital' is within range of καιριωτάτῳ. Mere preferences, not major errors.
